myriad

/MEER-ee-uhd/ - the stress falls on MEER · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Myriad means consisting of a very great number — so many that counting them is hopeless.

From the ferry's top deck the harbor's myriad lights ran together into one glowing smear, past any hope of counting.

Example

Open the hive and the myriad workers stop being individual bees at all: thirty, forty, fifty thousand bodies moving as one shimmering skin over the comb.

Myriad does the work 'many' can't: it asserts a number so great that counting stops being worth attempting. Fifty thousand bees aren't merely numerous — the tally collapses into a single shimmering impression, and myriad is the word for that.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

countless: Countless says flatly that counting is impossible — it is the everyday, plain-spoken twin. Myriad says the same thing in a higher register and often adds a shimmer of variety: myriad lights, myriad voices.

innumerable: Innumerable, like myriad, means too many to number, but it stays an ordinary adjective for bulk. Myriad carries its Greek history — the ten-thousand — and a literary flavor, which is why poems reach for myriad and reports for innumerable.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

few: a small number, easily counted at a glance

scant: barely sufficient in amount or number

Where it sits · how far past counting the number runs

numerous → myriad → infinite

numerous vs. myriad: Numerous is weaker than myriad: numerous complaints can still be logged and tallied one by one, while myriad complaints have outrun the tally entirely.

infinite vs. myriad: Infinite goes further than myriad — myriad things merely defeat the counting, but infinite things have no end at all, no matter how long the count runs.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — myri: countless; ten thousand (Greek myrios)

Suffix — -ad: group or unit of (as in monad and triad)

Put it together: Greek myrios meant 'countless'; its noun myrias pinned the word to the largest number Greek arithmetic bothered to name — ten thousand. A myriad of soldiers was first exactly 10,000 men; English kept only the older, wilder sense: too many to count.

Use the root in a new word: myriapod: My little brother came home from science camp announcing that he would only answer to 'the Myriapod' for the rest of the week.

Root Check

Word Choice

literary / formal

Myriad asserts number, not just variety: it says the count has outrun anyone's patience to finish it. A list you can actually complete — however varied — is numerous or assorted, not myriad. Both constructions are standard, and have been for centuries: 'myriad stars' and 'a myriad of stars' are equally good English.
